content.title: The 25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution: Frequently Asked Questions
content.text: The 25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution plays a crucial role in the continuity and stability of the executive branch. The amendment provides procedures for filling a vacancy in the vice presidency and addressing presidential incapacitation—either temporary or permanent—to ensure a process for determining who maintains the duties of the presidency. We address below frequently asked questions about the 25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution: When and why was the 25th Amendment ratified? What happens if a president is temporarily unable to perform the duties of the office? What happens if a president is permanently incapacitated and unable to perform the duties of the office? How is a vice-presidential vacancy filled? Can a president be removed from office against their will with the 25th Amendment? How many times has the 25th Amendment been invoked? When and why was the 25th Amendment ratified? The 25th Amendment was introduced after President John F. Kennedy’s assassination in 1963, which highlighted the need for more structured procedures for handling situations where the president is unable to perform their duties. Prior to its ratification by Congress in 1967, there was no definitive legal framework for addressing presidential disability despite numerous past instances where a president was significantly incapacitated. By this point, eight presidents and seven vice presidents had died in office, leaving the role of vice president vacant for the remainder of their terms. What happens if a president is temporarily unable to perform the duties of the office? Under Section 3 of the 25th Amendment, the president may voluntarily transfer power to the vice president by declaring in writing their inability to perform the duties of the office. The vice president then serves as acting president until the president declares in writing that they can resume their duties. What happens if a president is permanently incapacitated and unable to perform the duties of the office? Section 1 of the 25th Amendment resolves any ambiguity regarding the transfer of executive power by clarifying that if a president is removed from office, dies, or resigns, the vice president becomes the president. How is a vice-presidential vacancy filled? Section 2 of the 25th Amendment requires that if the office of the vice president becomes vacant, the president nominates a new vice president who must then be confirmed by a majority vote of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. This provision ensures that the office of the vice president is never left unoccupied for long. Can a president be removed from office against their will with the 25th Amendment? Section 4 of the 25th Amendment—perhaps the most complex part of the amendment, which has never been invoked—allows for the vice president and a majority of cabinet secretaries (or another body as Congress may provide) to declare the president unable to discharge the powers and duties of the office. The vice president then immediately assumes the role of acting president. If the president chooses to contest this declaration, Congress must then assemble to decide the issue within 48 hours (during which the vice president continues to serve as acting president). If two-thirds of both houses of Congress agree that the president is unable to perform their duties, the vice president continues as acting president; otherwise, the president resumes their duties. How many times has the 25th Amendment been invoked? Section 2 of the 25th Amendment has been invoked twice, both times within the decade following the amendment’s ratification. Upon the resignation of Vice President Spiro Agnew, President Richard Nixon nominated then-House Minority Leader Gerald Ford to the role of vice president, who was confirmed by the House and Senate. President Nixon resigned within the following year, promoting Ford to the presidency where he nominated Nelson Rockefeller as vice president for the remainder of the term. Section 3 has been invoked several times to ensure smooth operation of the executive branch in situations where the president is temporarily incapacitated. These include: President Ronald Reagan invoked the amendment in 1985 while he underwent surgery, temporarily transferring power to Vice President George H.W. Bush. President George W. Bush invoked Section 3 twice during his administration while he underwent routine medical procedures. President Joe Biden invoked Section 3 of the 25th Amendment to undergo a brief medical procedure in November 2021.
